slides.heading: Why a whole branch for one element?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — Organic chemistry is the chemistry of **carbon compounds** (except a few simple ones such as CO₂ and carbonates). More than ten million are known: fuels, plastics, medicines, foods and the molecules of living cells. Two properties of the carbon atom explain this huge number.

slides.narration: Namaste! Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds. Millions of them are known, from the gas in a kitchen cylinder to the proteins in your body. No other element comes close. In this part we find out why carbon is so special, how carbon atoms join to one another, and how to draw the structures of simple hydrocarbons.

slides.heading: Tetravalency
slides.body_md: Carbon (atomic number 6) has the configuration **2, 4**. To reach an octet it would have to lose or gain four electrons, which needs too much energy, so it **shares** its four valence electrons. Carbon therefore forms **four covalent bonds**: it is **tetravalent**. In methane, CH₄, the four bonds point to the corners of a regular **tetrahedron**.

headers: Electrons shared to complete the shell

visual.alt: Table of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and hydrogen with their configurations and the number of covalent bonds each forms

slides.narration: Carbon has six electrons, arranged two and four. Losing or gaining four electrons would take far too much energy, so carbon shares its four outer electrons instead. That is why it always forms four covalent bonds, a property called tetravalency. Compare nitrogen, which forms three bonds, oxygen, which forms two, and hydrogen, which forms just one.

slides.heading: Catenation
slides.body_md: **Catenation** is the ability of atoms of an element to **link with one another** by covalent bonds to form **long chains, branched chains and rings**. Carbon shows it far more than any other element, because carbon atoms are **small** and the **C–C bond is strong**. With four bonds per atom, every carbon in a chain still has bonds left over for hydrogen or other atoms.

visual.alt: Table of carbon compounds with chains of increasing length and where they are found

slides.narration: Catenation means atoms of the same element joining to one another in chains and rings. Carbon atoms are small and the bond between two carbon atoms is strong, so carbon can build chains of almost any length. Methane has one carbon atom, the gases in a cooking cylinder have three or four, petrol contains chains of about eight, and candle wax has chains of twenty or more.

slides.narration: Two carbon atoms may share one, two or three pairs of electrons. One shared pair is a single bond, as in ethane. Two pairs make a double bond, as in ethene, and three pairs make a triple bond, as in ethyne. Count the bonds around any carbon atom in these molecules and you always get four, because a double bond counts as two and a triple bond as three.

slides.heading: Worked example: counting bonds in propyne
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Propyne has the structure H–C≡C–CH₃. Find (a) the number of C–H bonds, (b) the number of shared pairs between carbon atoms and (c) the total number of shared pairs. Check that each carbon has four bonds.

**Step 1.** C–H bonds: 1 on the first carbon + 3 on the last = **4**.

**Step 2.** C≡C has 3 pairs and C–C has 1 pair: **4 pairs** between carbons.

**Step 3.** Total shared pairs: $4 + 4 = 8$.

**Check.** First C: 1 + 3 = 4; middle C: 3 + 1 = 4; last C: 1 + 3 = 4.

visual.alt: Table counting the bonds on each of the three carbon atoms of propyne, each totalling four

slides.narration: Start with the bonds to hydrogen: the first carbon has one and the methyl group at the end has three, making four. Between the carbon atoms there is a triple bond, which is three shared pairs, and a single bond, which is one more. So there are eight shared pairs in all. Finally check each carbon: every one of them has exactly four bonds.

slides.heading: Saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons
slides.body_md: **Hydrocarbons** contain only carbon and hydrogen. **Saturated** hydrocarbons (alkanes) have **only single bonds** between carbon atoms. **Unsaturated** hydrocarbons have at least one **double** (alkenes) or **triple** (alkynes) bond. Each family has its own **general formula** ($n$ = number of carbon atoms):

visual.alt: Table of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes with the bond present, general formula and first member

slides.narration: Hydrocarbons are compounds of carbon and hydrogen only. If every carbon to carbon bond is single, the hydrocarbon is saturated and belongs to the alkanes. If there is a double bond it is an alkene, and if there is a triple bond it is an alkyne; both are unsaturated. Each family has a general formula, so you can write any member once you know its number of carbon atoms.

slides.heading: Straight, branched and closed chains
slides.body_md:
Carbon atoms can be arranged in three ways:

- **Straight chain** (open chain, unbranched): every carbon is joined to at most two others in a row — pentane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃.
- **Branched chain**: a side chain is attached to the main chain — 2-methylbutane, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃.
- **Closed chain (cyclic)**: the carbon atoms form a **ring** — benzene, C₆H₆.

slides.narration: Carbon atoms can line up in a single row, which we call a straight chain. A chain can also carry a side branch, giving a branched chain. Or the ends of a chain can join to make a ring, which is a closed or cyclic chain. In this course the only ring compound you need is benzene, with six carbon atoms in its ring.

slides.heading: Quick check: types of chain
slides.body_md: Classify a carbon chain from its condensed formula.
slides.narration: Quick check. Look along the chain for a carbon atom joined to three other carbon atoms. If you find one, the chain has a side branch. If every carbon has at most two carbon neighbours, the chain is straight.

slides.heading: The structure of benzene
slides.body_md: **Benzene**, C₆H₆, is a **cyclic** hydrocarbon. Its six carbon atoms form a flat **hexagonal ring** joined by **alternate single and double bonds**, and each carbon carries **one hydrogen atom**. Each carbon makes four bonds: one to H, one single bond and one double bond to its two carbon neighbours. Books often draw just the hexagon; every corner is a CH group.

slides.narration: Benzene has six carbon atoms arranged in a flat ring shaped like a hexagon. Single and double bonds alternate around the ring, and every carbon atom carries one hydrogen atom. Check any carbon and you will find four bonds: one to hydrogen, a single bond to one neighbour and a double bond to the other. The shorthand hexagon means exactly the same thing.

slides.heading: Structural formulae up to five carbons
slides.body_md: A **molecular formula** gives only the number of atoms (C₄H₁₀). A **structural formula** shows how they are joined. The **condensed** form writes each carbon with its hydrogens: CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃. Write the carbon chain first, put in the multiple bond, then add hydrogens so that **every carbon has four bonds**.

visual.alt: Table of condensed structural formulae of straight-chain alkanes, alkenes and alkynes with two to five carbon atoms

slides.narration: A molecular formula only counts the atoms. A structural formula shows how they are linked. To write one, draw the carbon chain first, put in the double or triple bond where it belongs, and then add hydrogen atoms until every carbon has four bonds. The table shows straight chains of two to five carbon atoms for each family.

slides.heading: Worked example: five carbons, three families
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write the condensed structural formula and the molecular formula of a straight chain of five carbon atoms with (a) only single bonds, (b) a double bond between C1 and C2, (c) a triple bond between C2 and C3.

**(a)** CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃, **C₅H₁₂** (pentane).

**(b)** CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃, **C₅H₁₀** (pent-1-ene).

**(c)** CH₃–C≡C–CH₂–CH₃, **C₅H₈** (pent-2-yne).

Each multiple bond removes **two** hydrogen atoms.

visual.alt: Table counting the hydrogen atoms for the three five-carbon structures and matching each to its general formula

slides.narration: Draw five carbon atoms in a row each time. With only single bonds, each end carbon takes three hydrogens and each middle carbon two, giving twelve. A double bond at the start leaves the first two carbons with fewer hydrogens, giving ten. A triple bond in the second position takes away two more, giving eight. Each formula fits its family general formula.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Carbon (2, 4) shares four electrons: it is tetravalent.
Catenation: carbon atoms link into chains, branches and rings.
Single (one pair), double (two pairs) and triple (three pairs) C–C bonds; every carbon makes four bonds.
Chains are straight, branched or closed (cyclic); benzene is a ring of six CH groups with alternate double bonds.
Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.

rows: At least one C=C or C≡C

visual.alt: Summary table of tetravalency, catenation, saturated and unsaturated

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Carbon shares its four outer electrons and so forms four bonds. Its atoms link to one another in chains, branches and rings. Carbon atoms can share one, two or three pairs of electrons, giving single, double and triple bonds. Alkanes, alkenes and alkynes each follow their own general formula, and benzene is a ring of six carbon atoms.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: In a structural formula, count four bonds round every carbon before you move on.
A double bond counts as two bonds and a triple bond as three.
Draw benzene with six C and six H and alternate double bonds.
Carbon forms covalent bonds because losing or gaining four electrons needs too much energy.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. After drawing any structure, count the bonds around each carbon and make sure there are exactly four. Remember that a double bond counts as two and a triple bond as three. Draw benzene with six carbons, six hydrogens and alternate double bonds. And keep the two words apart: tetravalency is four bonds, catenation is self-linking.

slides.heading: Structural isomerism: chain isomers
slides.body_md: **Structural isomerism**: compounds with the **same molecular formula** but **different structural formulae**. In **chain isomerism**, the isomers differ in the **carbon skeleton** (straight or branched). C₄H₁₀ has **two** chain isomers; C₅H₁₂ has **three**: pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane. Isomers have the same molecular mass but different physical properties; more branching gives a lower boiling point.

slides.narration: Position isomers keep the same carbon chain but move the double bond, the triple bond or the functional group to a different carbon. With four carbon atoms in a row, the double bond can start at carbon one or carbon two, giving but one ene and but two ene. Propene has no position isomer, because a double bond at either end of a three carbon chain is the same molecule turned round.

slides.heading: Worked example: isomers or the same compound?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Say whether each pair are chain isomers, position isomers or the same compound.

**(a)** CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃ and CH₃–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₃

**(b)** CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ and CH₃–C(CH₃)₂–CH₃

**(c)** CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–Cl and CH₃–CHCl–CH₃

**Answer.** (a) **Same compound** (2-methylbutane, numbered from opposite ends). (b) **Chain isomers** (both C₅H₁₂). (c) **Position isomers** (1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane).

rows: Yes, branch on C2 either way

visual.alt: Decision table for three pairs of structures: same compound, chain isomers and position isomers

slides.narration: First check the molecular formula; if it differs, they are not isomers at all. In the first pair, the branch is on the second carbon whichever end you count from, so it is one compound written two ways. In the second pair the skeletons differ, so they are chain isomers. In the third, the chain is the same but the chlorine has moved, so they are position isomers.

slides.heading: Homologous series
slides.body_md: A **homologous series** is a family of organic compounds with the **same functional group** and the **same general formula**, in which successive members differ by a **CH₂** group (**14 u**). Members have **similar chemical properties** and show a **gradual change (gradation) in physical properties**: melting point, boiling point and density rise with molecular mass. They can be prepared by **similar methods**.

visual.alt: Table of the first five alkanes with formula, molecular mass, boiling point and state, showing masses rising by fourteen and boiling points rising

slides.narration: A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same functional group and the same general formula. Each member has one more carbon and two more hydrogen atoms than the one before, so the molecular mass goes up by fourteen each time. Their chemical reactions are alike, while boiling points rise steadily. Notice how the first four alkanes are gases but pentane is a liquid.

slides.heading: Functional groups
slides.body_md: A **functional group** is an atom or group of atoms that decides the **characteristic chemical properties** of a compound. Each has its own ending (suffix) or beginning (prefix) in the IUPAC name.

visual.alt: Table of nine classes of organic compounds with functional group, naming ending or prefix and an example

slides.narration: A functional group is the part of a molecule that decides how it reacts. The hydroxyl group makes an alcohol, the aldehyde group an aldehyde, the carbonyl group inside a chain a ketone, and the carboxyl group a carboxylic acid. Halogens, ethers and esters have groups of their own. Every group has its own ending or prefix in the systematic name, so the name tells you the family.

slides.heading: IUPAC naming: the four steps
slides.body_md:
1. **Word root** from the longest chain containing the functional group: meth (1), eth (2), prop (3), but (4), pent (5).
2. **Number** the chain from the end **nearer the functional group** (or multiple bond, or branch) so it gets the **lowest number**.
3. **Primary suffix**: -ane, -ene or -yne for the bonds in the chain.
4. **Secondary suffix** or **prefix** for the group, with its number: butan-2-ol, 2-chloropropane, 2-methylbutane.

nodes.label: Longest chain with the group → word root
Number from the end nearer the group
Add the group ending or prefix with its number

visual.alt: Flow of the four steps of IUPAC naming: word root, numbering, primary suffix, then group ending or prefix

slides.narration: Naming follows four steps. Find the longest carbon chain that contains the functional group; its length gives the word root, from meth for one carbon to pent for five. Number the chain from the end nearer the group so that it gets the lowest number. Add the ending for the bonds in the chain. Finally add the ending or prefix for the group, with its number.

slides.heading: Worked example: naming from a structure
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name (a) CH₃–CH₂–CH(OH)–CH₃, (b) CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃, (c) CH₃–CH₂–CO–CH₃, (d) CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–COOH.

**(a)** 4 carbons; number from the right so OH is on C2: **butan-2-ol**.

**(b)** 5 carbons, C=C from C1: **pent-1-ene**.

**(c)** 4 carbons, C=O on C2: **butan-2-one** (butanone).

**(d)** 4 carbons, the –COOH carbon is C1: **butanoic acid**.

visual.alt: Table naming four compounds by root, group position and full IUPAC name

slides.narration: In the first compound the chain has four carbons and the hydroxyl group is on the second carbon from the right, so it is butan two ol. The second has five carbons with the double bond starting at carbon one: pent one ene. The third is a four carbon ketone: butan two one. In the acid, the carbon of the carboxyl group is always carbon one, so no number is needed.

slides.heading: Worked example: from name to structure
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Draw condensed structures for (a) 2-bromopropane, (b) pentan-3-one, (c) methoxyethane, (d) ethyl methanoate.

**(a)** CH₃–CHBr–CH₃

**(b)** CH₃–CH₂–CO–CH₂–CH₃

**(c)** CH₃–O–CH₂–CH₃

**(d)** HCOO–CH₂–CH₃

**Method.** Write the chain from the root, number it, place the group at the stated carbon, then fill in hydrogens to give each carbon four bonds.

visual.alt: Table turning four IUPAC names into condensed structures

slides.narration: Read each name from the back. Propane means three carbons, and two bromo puts a bromine atom on the middle one. Pentan three one is a five carbon chain with the carbonyl group on the third carbon. Methoxyethane is a methoxy group joined through oxygen to an ethane chain. In ethyl methanoate, the acid part has one carbon and the ethyl group sits on the oxygen.

slides.heading: Trivial and IUPAC names
slides.body_md: Many compounds were named long before the IUPAC system. These **trivial (common) names** are still used, so learn both.

visual.alt: Table of nine common organic compounds with formula, trivial name and IUPAC name

slides.narration: Many organic compounds had everyday names long before the modern rules. Ethyl alcohol is ethanol, acetic acid is ethanoic acid, formaldehyde is methanal and acetone is propanone. Ethylene and acetylene are the old names of ethene and ethyne. Exam questions use both kinds of name, so learn them in pairs.

slides.heading: Quick check: IUPAC names
slides.body_md: Name a compound from its condensed formula.
slides.narration: Quick check. Count all the carbon atoms in the chain, including the carbon of the functional group itself. That gives the word root. Then identify the functional group and pick the ending that belongs to it.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Isomers: same molecular formula, different structures.
Chain isomers differ in the carbon skeleton (C₄H₁₀: 2; C₅H₁₂: 3); position isomers differ in where the bond or group sits.
Homologous series: same functional group and general formula, differ by CH₂ (14 u), similar chemistry, graded physical properties.
IUPAC name = position + prefix + word root + primary suffix + secondary suffix.
Know the trivial names: ethyl alcohol, acetic acid, formaldehyde, acetone, ethylene, acetylene.

visual.alt: Summary table of chain isomers, position isomers and homologues

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Isomers have the same formula but different structures. Chain isomers differ in their skeleton, and position isomers differ in where the bond or group is placed. A homologous series is a family that differs by one carbon and two hydrogens at a time. IUPAC names are built from a root, endings and numbers, and you should know the common names too.

Number the chain to give the functional group, then the multiple bond, then the branch, the lowest number.
Aldehyde and acid carbons are always C1, so butanal and butanoic acid need no number.
Older books write 1-butene or 2-propanol; the current style is but-1-ene and propan-2-ol.

rows: Not possible: an aldehyde is always at C1
Methoxyethane (larger group is the parent chain)

Give the lowest number to the functional group first. Aldehyde and carboxylic acid groups are always on carbon one, so they need no number. You may see older names like one butene; the modern form puts the number just before the ending.

notes.title: Organic Chemistry: Introduction, Structure, Isomerism and Nomenclature — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The unique nature of carbon
sections.body_md:
**Organic chemistry** is the chemistry of carbon compounds (other than oxides of carbon, carbonates and a few others). Over ten million are known, because of two properties of carbon:

- **Tetravalency:** carbon (2, 4) cannot easily lose or gain four electrons, so it **shares** them and forms **four covalent bonds**. In methane the four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron.
- **Catenation:** carbon atoms **link to one another** to form long chains, branched chains and rings, because the C–C bond is strong and the carbon atom is small.

Two carbon atoms can share one, two or three pairs of electrons: a **single** (C–C), **double** (C=C) or **triple** (C≡C) bond. Every carbon still has **four bonds in total**.

key_terms.definition_md: The property of carbon of forming four covalent bonds, by sharing its four valence electrons.
The property of atoms of an element of linking with one another by covalent bonds to form chains and rings.
A covalent bond in which two atoms share three pairs of electrons, as in ethyne.

visual.alt: Table of single, double and triple carbon–carbon bonds with the number of shared pairs and an example

sections.heading: 2. Straight, branched and cyclic chains; benzene
sections.body_md:
- **Straight (open, unbranched) chain:** CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ (butane).
- **Branched chain:** a side group on the main chain, CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₃ (2-methylpropane). A carbon joined to **three or four** other carbons marks a branch.
- **Closed chain (cyclic):** the chain closes into a ring.

**Benzene, C₆H₆:** a flat hexagonal ring of six carbon atoms with **alternate single and double bonds** (Kekulé structure); each carbon carries **one hydrogen atom**. It is the only ring compound in this chapter.

key_terms.definition_md: A carbon chain in which at least one carbon atom is bonded to three or four other carbon atoms.
A compound whose carbon atoms are joined in a closed ring, such as benzene.

visual.alt: Table classifying pentane, 2-methylbutane and benzene by type of chain

sections.heading: 3. Hydrocarbons and structural formulae
sections.body_md:
**Hydrocarbons** contain carbon and hydrogen only.

- **Saturated** (alkanes): only C–C single bonds.
- **Unsaturated**: at least one C=C (alkenes) or C≡C (alkynes).

A **molecular formula** counts the atoms; a **structural formula** shows how they are joined; a **condensed formula** writes each carbon with its hydrogens (CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃). To draw one: chain first, multiple bond next, then hydrogens until every carbon has four bonds. Each double bond removes two hydrogen atoms from the alkane formula; a triple bond removes four.

key_terms.definition_md: A hydrocarbon with only single bonds between carbon atoms.
A hydrocarbon with at least one carbon–carbon double or triple bond.
A formula that shows how the atoms in a molecule are bonded to one another.

visual.alt: Table of molecular formulae and names of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes with three to five carbon atoms

sections.heading: 4. Structural isomerism
sections.body_md:
**Isomers:** compounds with the **same molecular formula** but **different structural formulae** (and so different properties).

- **Chain isomers** differ in the carbon skeleton. C₄H₁₀: butane and 2-methylpropane. C₅H₁₂: pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane. More branching lowers the boiling point.
- **Position isomers** have the same skeleton but the multiple bond or functional group in a different position: but-1-ene and but-2-ene; propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol; 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane.

Methane, ethane, propane, ethene, propene and propyne have **no** chain or position isomers. Before calling two drawings isomers, number each chain from both ends — they may be the same compound.

key_terms.definition_md: The existence of two or more compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.
Isomers that differ in the arrangement of the carbon chain (straight or branched).
Isomers with the same carbon chain that differ in the position of a multiple bond or functional group.

visual.alt: Table of isomers of four formulae and the type of isomerism shown

sections.heading: 5. Homologous series
sections.body_md:
A **homologous series** is a group of organic compounds with the same functional group, in which successive members differ by a –CH₂– unit. Characteristics:

1. All members have the **same general formula** and the **same functional group**.
2. Successive members differ by **CH₂**, i.e. by **14 u** in molecular mass.
3. They have **similar chemical properties**.
4. Physical properties show **gradation**: melting point, boiling point and density increase with molecular mass (C₁–C₄ alkanes are gases, C₅ onwards liquids).
5. They can be prepared by **similar general methods**.

key_terms.definition_md: A series of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which successive members differ by a CH₂ group.
Members of the same homologous series, such as ethanol and propan-1-ol.

visual.alt: Table of four alkenes with formula and molecular mass, rising by fourteen each step

sections.heading: 6. Nomenclature: trivial and IUPAC names
sections.body_md:
**IUPAC name** = (position + prefix) + **word root** + **primary suffix** + (position + **secondary suffix**).

- **Word root** (longest chain containing the functional group): meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4, pent 5.
- **Numbering:** from the end nearer the functional group, then the multiple bond, then the branch — **lowest number**.
- **Primary suffix:** -ane, -ene, -yne. **Prefixes:** methyl-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-, methoxy-.
- **Secondary suffix:** -ol (alcohol), -al (aldehyde), -one (ketone), -oic acid (carboxylic acid). The final "e" of -ane is dropped before a vowel: ethan**ol**, propan**al**.
- **Ethers:** alkoxyalkane (smaller group as alkoxy): CH₃OC₂H₅ is methoxyethane. **Esters:** alkyl alkanoate: CH₃COOC₂H₅ is ethyl ethanoate.

Trivial names to know: methyl alcohol (methanol), ethyl alcohol (ethanol), formaldehyde (methanal), acetaldehyde (ethanal), acetone (propanone), formic acid (methanoic acid), acetic acid (ethanoic acid), ethylene (ethene), acetylene (ethyne), methyl chloride (chloromethane).

key_terms.definition_md: An atom or group of atoms that decides the characteristic chemical properties of an organic compound.
The part of an IUPAC name that gives the number of carbon atoms in the main chain, such as prop for three.

visual.alt: Table of five classes of compounds with functional group, an example and its IUPAC name

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Drawing a carbon with five bonds (for example CH₂=CH₂–CH₃); count four bonds round every carbon.
- Calling two drawings of the same molecule "isomers"; number both ways first.
- Numbering from the wrong end (3-methylbutane instead of 2-methylbutane; but-3-ene instead of but-1-ene).
- Giving a number to an aldehyde or acid group (it is always C1).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Structural formula (1 mark): every bond and every hydrogen shown correctly.
- IUPAC name (1 mark): correct root, ending and position number, with hyphens.
- Isomers (2–3 marks): one mark per correct structure with its name.

questions.stem_md: Carbon (atomic number 6) forms four covalent bonds in methane, CH₄. This is because a carbon atom:

options.text_md: loses four electrons to form a C⁴⁺ ion
gains four electrons to form a C⁴⁻ ion
has four valence electrons and shares all four of them to complete its octet

questions.solution_md: Configuration 2, 4: losing or gaining four electrons needs too much energy, so carbon shares its four valence electrons — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In pentane, CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃, five carbon atoms are bonded directly to one another in a chain. This ability of carbon atoms to link with each other is called:
questions.solution_md: Self-linking of carbon atoms into chains and rings is catenation — option (b).

questions.stem_md: How many electrons in total are shared between the two carbon atoms of ethyne, H–C≡C–H?
questions.solution_md: A triple bond is three shared pairs, that is six electrons — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Carbon readily forms C⁴⁻ ions in its compounds.

**Reason (R):** A carbon atom has four electrons in its outermost shell.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: a nucleus with six protons cannot easily hold ten electrons, so carbon shares electrons instead. R is true (configuration 2, 4) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Methane, CH₄, conducts electricity when liquefied, because the bonds in it are ionic.
questions.solution_md: False: the C–H bonds in methane are covalent; liquid methane contains molecules, not ions, so it does not conduct.

questions.stem_md: The property of carbon by which each of its atoms forms four covalent bonds is called ___.
questions.solution_md: **Tetravalency**: carbon (2, 4) shares its four valence electrons.

questions.stem_md: Write the electronic configuration of carbon (atomic number 6) and state the number of covalent bonds that one carbon atom forms.

answer.model_answer_md: Carbon: 2, 4. It forms four covalent bonds (it is tetravalent).

questions.solution_md: 2, 4; four bonds.

questions.stem_md: Define catenation.

answer.model_answer_md: Catenation is the property of atoms of an element (especially carbon) of linking with one another by covalent bonds to form long chains, branched chains or rings.

questions.solution_md: Definition.

questions.stem_md: A carbon atom forms neither a C⁴⁺ ion nor a C⁴⁻ ion. Give a reason why it does not (a) lose four electrons; (b) gain four electrons.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Removing four electrons would need a very large amount of energy, and a C⁴⁺ ion (six protons holding only two electrons) would be very unstable. (b) A nucleus of six protons cannot hold ten electrons firmly; adding four electrons needs a lot of energy because of strong repulsion between them. So carbon shares its electrons instead.

questions.solution_md: Energy needed in both cases; sharing instead.

questions.stem_md: The carbon chain in CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃ is:

options.text_md: a chain containing a double bond

questions.solution_md: The second carbon is joined to three other carbon atoms, so a side chain is present — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the Kekulé structure of benzene, C₆H₆, each carbon atom is joined to:

options.text_md: three carbon atoms and no hydrogen atom
two carbon atoms and two hydrogen atoms, with single bonds only
two carbon atoms and one hydrogen atom, with single and double bonds alternating round the ring
one carbon atom and three hydrogen atoms

questions.solution_md: Six carbon atoms form a hexagon of alternate single and double bonds; each carries one hydrogen, giving C₆H₆ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Every carbon atom in benzene, C₆H₆, is bonded to exactly one hydrogen atom.
questions.solution_md: True: six carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms; each ring carbon carries one hydrogen and uses its other three bonds in the ring (one single and one double bond).

questions.stem_md: Draw the structural formula of benzene.

answer.model_answer_md: A flat hexagonal ring of six carbon atoms joined by alternate single and double bonds (C=C, C–C, C=C, C–C, C=C, C–C), with one hydrogen atom bonded to each carbon atom.

questions.solution_md: Hexagon with alternate double bonds; six H.

marking_scheme.step: Ring with alternate double bonds and six H

questions.stem_md: State whether the carbon chain in (CH₃)₂CH–CH₂–CH₃ is straight, branched or cyclic. Give a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: Branched: the second carbon atom (the CH) is bonded to three other carbon atoms. (The compound is 2-methylbutane.)

questions.solution_md: Branched.

questions.stem_md: A straight-chain hydrocarbon has four carbon atoms and one carbon–carbon triple bond. Its molecular formula is:
questions.solution_md: Alkyne CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ with n = 4 gives C₄H₆ (but-1-yne or but-2-yne) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Pent-2-ene, CH₃–CH=CH–CH₂–CH₃, is described as an unsaturated hydrocarbon because it:
questions.solution_md: Unsaturated means at least one C=C or C≡C bond — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The hydrocarbon with the condensed formula CH₃–C≡C–CH₃ is:
questions.solution_md: Four carbons (but-), a triple bond (-yne) starting at C2 from either end — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Calculate the percentage by mass of carbon in propyne, C₃H₄. (C = 12, H = 1)
questions.solution_md: Molecular mass of propyne $= 3 \times 12 + 4 \times 1 = 40$. Mass of carbon $= 3 \times 12 = 36$. Percentage of carbon $= \frac{36}{40} \times 100 = 90$, so carbon is 90 per cent of the mass.

questions.stem_md: Draw the structural formula of pent-1-yne.

answer.model_answer_md: CH≡C–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃: a chain of five carbon atoms with a triple bond between C1 and C2; C1 carries one H, C3 and C4 two H each, and C5 three H (C₅H₈).

questions.solution_md: Triple bond at C1.

questions.stem_md: Draw the structural formula of propene, showing every bond.

answer.model_answer_md: CH₂=CH–CH₃ drawn in full: C1 has two H atoms and a double bond to C2; C2 has one H atom and a single bond to C3; C3 has three H atoms (C₃H₆).

questions.solution_md: Displayed formula of propene.

marking_scheme.step: All bonds and six H shown

questions.stem_md:
Complete each sentence by choosing the correct word from the bracket.

(a) The general formula of the alkenes is ___ (CₙH₂ₙ / CₙH₂ₙ₋₂).

(b) A hydrocarbon in which every carbon–carbon bond is a single bond is ___ (saturated / unsaturated).

(c) Ethyne contains a ___ (double / triple) bond between its two carbon atoms.
questions.solution_md: (a) **CₙH₂ₙ**; (b) **saturated**; (c) **triple**.

questions.stem_md: Butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, and 2-methylpropane, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃, both have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀. They are:
questions.solution_md: Same formula, different carbon skeletons (straight and branched) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, and propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, are:
questions.solution_md: Same three-carbon chain and formula C₃H₈O; only the position of –OH differs — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which formula represents the same compound as CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃?
questions.solution_md: Read from the other end, CH₃–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₃ is again a four-carbon chain with a methyl group on C2: both are 2-methylbutane — option (d).

questions.stem_md: How many chain isomers have the molecular formula C₅H₁₂?
questions.solution_md: Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** But-1-ene and but-2-ene are position isomers.

**Reason (R):** They have the same molecular formula and the same carbon chain, but the double bond is in a different position.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R is the definition of position isomerism applied to A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Butane and 2-methylpropane have the same molecular mass.

**Reason (R):** Butane and 2-methylpropane are position isomers.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true (both C₄H₁₀, 58). R is false: they differ in the carbon skeleton, so they are chain isomers — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Propene, C₃H₆, has a straight-chain position isomer in which the double bond lies between carbon atoms 2 and 3.
questions.solution_md: False: CH₃–CH=CH₂ numbered from the other end is CH₂=CH–CH₃, the same molecule, so propene has no position isomer.

questions.stem_md: Name the position isomer of but-1-ene and write its condensed formula.

answer.model_answer_md: But-2-ene, CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃.

questions.solution_md: But-2-ene.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by structural isomerism?

answer.model_answer_md: Structural isomerism: two or more compounds have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae (different arrangements of atoms).

questions.solution_md: Definition.

questions.stem_md: Draw the structural formulae of the two chain isomers of C₄H₁₀ and give the IUPAC name of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Butane: CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ (straight chain). 2-methylpropane: CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₃ (a three-carbon chain with a methyl group on C2).

questions.solution_md: Two structures with names.

questions.stem_md: Draw the three chain isomers of C₅H₁₂ and name each by the IUPAC system. Which of them has the lowest boiling point?

answer.model_answer_md: Pentane: CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃. 2-methylbutane: CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃. 2,2-dimethylpropane: CH₃–C(CH₃)₂–CH₃. The most branched, 2,2-dimethylpropane, has the lowest boiling point.

questions.solution_md: Three structures and names; most branched boils lowest.

questions.stem_md: A student named a compound "3-methylbutane". (a) Draw the structure that this name describes. (b) Give the correct IUPAC name and state the rule the student broke.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) A four-carbon chain with a methyl group on C3: CH₃–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₃. (b) Numbering from the other end puts the methyl group on C2, so the correct name is 2-methylbutane. The chain must be numbered from the end that gives the substituent the lowest number.

questions.solution_md: Structure; 2-methylbutane; lowest-number rule.

questions.stem_md: In the alkene series, the member that comes just after propene, C₃H₆, has the molecular formula:
questions.solution_md: Add CH₂: C₃H₆ + CH₂ = C₄H₈ (but-1-ene), which fits CₙH₂ₙ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The boiling points of methane, ethane and propane are −162 °C, −89 °C and −42 °C. The boiling point of butane, the next straight-chain alkane, is most likely to be about:
questions.solution_md: Boiling point rises steadily with molecular mass, by a smaller step each time (73 then 47 degrees), so the next value is a little below 0 °C — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Methanol, ethanol and propan-1-ol belong to one homologous series. Which of the following is nearly the same for all three?

options.text_md: Their chemical reactions, such as the reaction with sodium

questions.solution_md: Members share a functional group, so their chemical properties are similar; physical properties change gradually — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Methanal, HCHO, and ethanal, CH₃CHO, belong to the same homologous series.
questions.solution_md: True: both have the –CHO (aldehyde) group and differ by one CH₂ unit.

questions.stem_md: Two successive members of any homologous series differ in formula by one ___ unit.
questions.solution_md: **CH₂** (a difference of 14 u in molecular mass).

questions.stem_md: An alkene has a molecular mass of 70. How many carbon atoms are there in one molecule of it? (C = 12, H = 1)
questions.solution_md: An alkene is CₙH₂ₙ, so its molecular mass is $12n + 2n = 14n$. Then $14n = 70$, so $n = \frac{70}{14} = 5$. The alkene has 5 carbon atoms (C₅H₁₀, for example pent-1-ene).

questions.stem_md: What is the molecular mass of 2,2-dimethylpropane? (C = 12, H = 1)
questions.solution_md: 2,2-dimethylpropane is a chain isomer of pentane, C₅H₁₂. Molecular mass $= 5 \times 12 + 12 \times 1 = 72$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Pentane is a liquid at room temperature, while propane is a gas.

**Reason (R):** All the members of a homologous series have the same general formula.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A: pentane is a liquid because its larger molecular mass gives it a higher boiling point (gradation of physical properties) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Write the molecular formula and the IUPAC name of the alkyne that comes just after propyne in its homologous series.

answer.model_answer_md: C₄H₆, but-1-yne.

questions.solution_md: C₃H₄ + CH₂.

questions.stem_md: Write the general formula of the alkanes, and use it to write the molecular formula of the alkane with five carbon atoms.

answer.model_answer_md: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; with n = 5, C₅H₁₂ (pentane).

questions.solution_md: General formula; C₅H₁₂.

questions.stem_md: Ethene, propene and but-1-ene are members of one homologous series. (a) Give two characteristics of a homologous series shown by these three compounds. (b) Write the general formula of this series.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Any two: they have the same functional group (C=C); successive members differ by CH₂ (14 u); they have similar chemical properties (for example, all add hydrogen); their boiling points rise from ethene to but-1-ene. (b) CₙH₂ₙ.

questions.solution_md: Two characteristics; CₙH₂ₙ.

questions.stem_md: The IUPAC name of CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CHO is:
questions.solution_md: Four carbons including the –CHO carbon, aldehyde ending -al — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The IUPAC name of CH₃–CH(Cl)–CH₂–CH₃ is:
questions.solution_md: Four-carbon chain; numbering from the left puts Cl on C2, the lower number — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The ester CH₃COOCH₃ is named:
questions.solution_md: The acid part CH₃COO– has two carbons (ethanoate); the group on the oxygen is methyl — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Formaldehyde, HCHO, a preservative for biological specimens, has the IUPAC name:
questions.solution_md: One carbon (meth-) with the aldehyde ending -al — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The IUPAC name of CH₃–O–CH₂–CH₃ is:

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain the terms tetravalency and catenation. [2]

(b) Draw the structural formula of benzene and state its molecular formula. [2]

(c) Classify each chain as straight, branched or cyclic: (i) CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃, (ii) CH₃–C(CH₃)₂–CH₃, (iii) C₆H₆ (benzene). [3]

(d) Draw the structural formulae, showing every bond, of (i) ethane, (ii) ethene and (iii) ethyne, and state the number of electron pairs shared between the two carbon atoms in each. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Tetravalency: carbon (2, 4) shares its four valence electrons and so forms four covalent bonds. Catenation: carbon atoms link with one another by covalent bonds to form chains, branches and rings.

(b) A hexagonal ring of six carbon atoms with alternate single and double bonds and one hydrogen on each carbon. Molecular formula C₆H₆.

(c) (i) Straight. (ii) Branched (the central carbon is joined to four carbons). (iii) Cyclic.

(d) (i) Ethane H₃C–CH₃ with three H on each carbon: one pair. (ii) Ethene H₂C=CH₂ with two H on each carbon: two pairs. (iii) Ethyne H–C≡C–H: three pairs.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define structural isomerism and name the two kinds of structural isomerism you have studied. [2]

(b) Draw the structural formulae of the two chain isomers of butane and name them. [2]

(c) Draw and name the two straight-chain position isomers of C₄H₆. State the class of compound to which they belong. [3]

(d) Give a reason for each: (i) CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃ and CH₃–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₃ are not isomers of each other; (ii) propene has no position isomer; (iii) 2-methylpropane boils at a lower temperature than butane. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae are structural isomers. Kinds: chain isomerism and position isomerism.

(b) Butane CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃; 2-methylpropane CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₃.

(c) But-1-yne CH≡C–CH₂–CH₃ and but-2-yne CH₃–C≡C–CH₃. They are alkynes.

(d) (i) Both are a four-carbon chain with a methyl group on C2, numbered from opposite ends: they are the same compound, 2-methylbutane. (ii) In a three-carbon chain a double bond at either end gives the same molecule, CH₂=CH–CH₃. (iii) The branched molecule is more compact, so the attraction between its molecules is weaker and less energy is needed to boil it.

questions.solution_md: Definition and kinds; two isomers; two alkynes; three reasons.

(c) The boiling points of the first four straight-chain alkanes are −162 °C, −89 °C, −42 °C and −1 °C. (i) Describe and explain the trend. (ii) Pentane boils at 36 °C. State its physical state at 25 °C. (iii) Calculate the molecular mass of pentane. (C = 12, H = 1) [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A series of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which successive members differ by a CH₂ group. Characteristics (any two): same general formula; differ by 14 u; similar chemical properties; gradation in physical properties; similar methods of preparation.

(b) (i) C₃H₈, propane. (ii) C₄H₈, but-1-ene. (iii) C₅H₈, pent-1-yne.

(c) (i) The boiling point rises from methane to butane as the molecular mass (chain length) increases, because larger molecules attract one another more strongly. (ii) Liquid (25 °C is below its boiling point). (iii) Pentane is C₅H₁₂: $5 \times 12 + 12 \times 1 = 72$.
